source.title: Scaling Collapse Reveals Universal Dynamics in Compute-Optimally Trained Neural Networks
source.authors: Shi-Kai Qiu; Lechao Xiao; Andrew Gordon Wilson; Jeffrey Pennington; Atish Agarwala

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Measures loss scaling and compute-optimal training horizons across model sizes, using test loss and power-law fits in small-scale tasks. This bears on scaling claims, but the experiments are not a direct replication of the original large language-model studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports power-law fits for loss versus compute and joint loss-versus-tokens-and-parameters fits, plus estimates of compute-optimal training horizons. It also reports how collapse changes with learning-rate schedule, parameterization, compute allocation, and the loss offset used for normalization. Its shared-parameter loss-curve predictions across schedules are not predictions from power laws fitted on small runs, so they do not test V2. Depth scaling is reported, but it does not compare depth and width at fixed parameter count as V4 requires. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper's main subject is normalized loss-curve collapse. Its own experiments still fit power-law compute-optimal frontiers, sum-of-power-laws loss surfaces and compute-optimal data exponents. These were run in new, small-scale settings: CIFAR-5M pixel-token transformers, chess next-move transformers and MLP synthetic regression. That makes it T3 for V5, with T3 evidence on V3 and on V7's schedule-dependence. No natural-language pretraining is run, so it does not test V1 as stated, which concerns language models.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that compute-optimally trained models of different sizes have normalized loss curves that collapse onto one universal curve, and that learning-rate decay makes the collapse tighter than the seed noise (supercollapse). They present collapse as a sensitive diagnostic of correct hyperparameter scaling. They explain the effect through sum-of-power-laws scaling, which accounts for collapse under a constant learning rate, and through an SGD-noise model that predicts loss under different schedules. They call the experiments a small-scale proof of concept and the theory approximate.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits compute-optimal loss frontiers and power-law loss relations, including a Pareto-frontier procedure similar to prior compute-optimal work. It differs by focusing on normalized full training curves and small-scale tasks, rather than reproducing the original large language-model experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Collapse changes with learning-rate schedule, parameterization (µP versus constant learning rate), compute-optimal data exponent, and the loss offset L̂ used for normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Normalized loss curves from compute-optimally trained models of different sizes collapse onto one curve, tighter than the seed noise floor under learning-rate decay. The collapse breaks with a suboptimal data exponent, constant learning rate instead of µP, or a wrong loss offset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal training yields scale-invariant normalized loss curves (supercollapse), and the quality of collapse diagnoses hyperparameter scaling more sensitively than final loss.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267 (2025)
record.problems: The empirical models are small-scale proxies, not large natural-language models. The compute-optimal horizons are estimated from Pareto frontiers using a limited model ladder and a fit that drops the smallest and largest model points. Some results are figure-based, and not every fit reports uncertainty. The authors also state that their theoretical analysis uses approximations and has limitations for nonlinear networks and adaptive optimizers.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Depthwise scaling in Appendix B was not recorded as a V4 result because it does not compare architecture details at fixed parameter count. Schedule-prediction results using the noise model were not recorded as V2 because they are not power-law extrapolations from small runs.

untested.parts: Not tested: no natural-language pretraining is run; all tasks are image tokens, chess or synthetic regression.
Not tested: no extrapolation of small-run power laws to much larger runs. The schedule-prediction model uses measured gradient covariance, not a power-law extrapolation.

Not tested: language models, and the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann comparison. No separate N_opt(C) and D_opt(C) fits are reported, and the allocation's stability beyond a model range under one decade is not checked.
Not tested: no comparison of depth versus width at a fixed parameter count. The depth ladder in Appendix B changes parameter count.
Not tested: video, fine-tuning and transfer. Repeated data is present (multi-epoch CIFAR-5M) but is not varied.
Not tested: effects of parameter-counting conventions and fitting methods on exponents, and disagreement between published laws.

missing.what: Compute-optimal power-law fit for the chess depth ladder (depths 9–36): a=0.355, b=0.164, L0=0.545.
A single shared α (0.21 for transformers, 0.26 for MLPs) predicts loss curves across schedules, model sizes and training horizons. Useful context on schedule-dependence of loss curves.
Data reuse: CIFAR-5M about 5B tokens trained for more than one epoch, and some chess reuse, with no significant train/test gap. This condition is relevant to the repeated-data regime.
missing.locator: Appendix A, 'Training for More than One Epoch'

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 links were removed because no language-model pretraining is run; the scaling fits bear on V5 instead. Collapse-quality rows r8–r10 measure a different construct and moved to fits_no_version. Tranche changed from T2 to T3, since these are new settings rather than a different method on the same LM question. The V3 evidence suggests equal growth of parameters and tokens (γ≈1), but only in non-language tasks over a model range under one decade.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests scaling on CIFAR-5M next-token prediction, chess next-move prediction, and synthetic regression, but not large-scale natural-language pretraining or separate one-variable sweeps where the other two quantities are explicitly non-bottlenecks.

No test of whether power laws fitted on small runs predict the loss of runs orders of magnitude larger. The paper’s schedule predictions use a measured gradient covariance and a shared fitted parameter, not small-run power-law extrapolation.

The paper fits compute-optimal compute as a power of parameter count and derives training horizons, but does not report separate parameter-count-versus-compute and token-count-versus-compute fits or test the Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann comparison.
Depth scaling is examined, but not architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count to measure how much depth, width, or other details change loss.

The reported settings include image-token prediction, chess next-move prediction, and synthetic regression. The paper does not test video models, fine-tuning, transfer, or establish the same law across a broad range of modalities and regimes.

The paper shows dependence on schedule, parameterization, compute allocation, and the loss offset used for collapse. It does not test whether published exponents disagree because of parameter-count conventions or fitting choices across the original studies, nor does it establish a general bend in final-loss scaling curves.

rows.subject: Transformers on CIFAR-5M
rows.operation_detail: Fit compute-optimal test loss to L0 + a c^-b
rows.note: The fit is shown for a transformer next-token prediction task on image-derived tokens; the figure labels the fitted scaling law.
rows.check: V1 is about language-model pretraining loss, but this is greyscale pixel prediction, so the row bears on V5 only. The run uses repeated data: about 5B tokens, trained for more than one epoch (Appendix A). Compute spans only about one decade (10^3 to 10^4 PFLOPs) and parameters 10M to 80M. No R² or uncertainty is given for this fit.

rows.subject: Transformers on CIFAR-5M
rows.operation_detail: Fit expected loss to a sum of token-count and parameter-count power laws
rows.measure: Expected loss as a function of training tokens and parameters
rows.value: L = 3.134 + t^-0.41 + p^-0.37; R² = 0.999 (constant multipliers not shown)
rows.note: The authors state the constant-learning-rate CIFAR-5M curves agree well with this sum-of-power-laws fit.
rows.check: Non-language image-token task, so V5 only, not V1. This is a joint tokens × parameters fit under a constant learning rate, with multi-epoch data reuse.

rows.subject: Transformers on chess
rows.operation_detail: Fit loss to a sum of token-count and parameter-count power laws
rows.measure: Loss as a function of training tokens and parameters
rows.value: L = 0.5465 + t^-0.28 + p^-0.21; R² = 0.998 (constant multipliers not shown)
rows.note: The paper says the chess fit is worse than the other displayed dataset fits.
rows.check: Character-level chess notation is not natural-language pretraining, so V5 only. The authors say the chess fit is worse than the other datasets.

rows.subject: MLPs on power-law Fourier features
rows.operation_detail: Fit loss to a sum of token-count and parameter-count power laws

conditions.value: synthetic regression with a power-law Fourier spectrum

rows.measure: Loss as a function of training examples and parameters
rows.value: L = 0 + t^-0.34 + p^-0.29; R² = 0.999 (constant multipliers not shown)
rows.note: The authors describe the irreducible loss as negligible for this task.
rows.check: Synthetic regression whose target is built to elicit power laws, so this is V5 only. The fit reflects the designed power-law spectrum.

rows.subject: Transformers on CIFAR-5M
rows.operation_detail: Fit compute-optimal compute c*(p) = κp^(1+γ), then infer the token horizon

conditions.value: Pareto frontier from constant-learning-rate runs; smallest and largest model points dropped as outliers

rows.note: The horizon is stated to scale as t*(p) = c*(p)/(6p), hence as p^γ.
rows.check: γ=0.96 means tokens grow roughly in proportion to parameters, a Hoffmann-like equal split. Smallest and largest models are dropped from the fit, no uncertainty is reported, and the setting is not a language model.

rows.subject: MLPs on power-law Fourier features
rows.operation_detail: Fit compute-optimal compute c*(p) = κp^(1+γ), then infer the token horizon

conditions.value: Pareto frontier from constant-learning-rate runs; smallest and largest model points dropped as outliers

rows.note: The horizon is stated to scale as t*(p) = c*(p)/(6p), hence as p^γ.
rows.check: γ=1.04 in synthetic MLP regression. Endpoint models are dropped and no uncertainty is reported.

rows.subject: Transformers on chess
rows.operation_detail: Estimate compute-optimal data exponent from the loss-compute Pareto frontier
rows.note: The text identifies 1.02 as the estimated compute-optimal value before showing the over-trained comparison.
rows.check: γ=1.02 on chess; no fit figure or uncertainty is shown.

rows.subject: Transformers on chess
rows.operation_detail: Increase the training-horizon data exponent above the estimated compute-optimal value
rows.measure: Alignment of normalized loss curves across model sizes
rows.baseline: Normalized loss curves with estimated compute-optimal data exponent 1.02 collapse strongly
rows.value: Increasing γ to 1.2 shifts normalized curves and breaks collapse
rows.note: The paper says larger models make more rapid relative initial progress and then decelerate later under the excessive exponent.
rows.check: This row measures loss-curve collapse quality, not loss or the allocation itself. Its 'absent' state does not map onto V3 or V7. The paper only says over-training gives a 'minor worsening in the scaling law', with no number.

rows.subject: MLPs on power-law Fourier features
rows.operation_detail: Replace µP learning-rate scaling with one constant learning rate across widths

conditions.value: constant learning rate across model widths

rows.measure: Collapse of normalized loss curves across widths
rows.value: Constant learning rate across widths breaks collapse
rows.note: The text says final losses at small scales are virtually identical between the constant-rate and µP settings, while the normalized curves differ.
rows.check: Collapse quality under a different parameterization is not a scaling-law measure. The authors say final losses are virtually identical at small scales.

rows.subject: Transformers on CIFAR-5M
rows.operation_detail: Compare collapse under different subtracted loss offsets L̂
rows.baseline: L̂ = L0 = 3.132 gives the best collapse
rows.value: Offsets far from L0 break the collapse; plotted alternatives include 3.12 and 3.14
rows.note: The text explicitly states that setting L̂ far from L0 breaks collapse; the curves for the listed offsets are shown in the figure.
rows.check: The choice of offset in the collapse normalization is a choice in the study's own diagnostic, not a fitting choice for a scaling law.

rows.subject: Transformers on CIFAR-5M
rows.operation_detail: Assess whether the sum-of-power-laws loss form fits curves under different learning-rate schedules

conditions.value: most tested schedules other than constant learning rate

rows.measure: Fit of the loss curve to the sum-of-power-laws form
rows.baseline: The sum-of-power-laws form fits the constant-learning-rate curves
rows.value: The form fails to fit empirical loss curves with most learning-rate schedules
rows.note: The paper says schedules can modulate curve shape and that the resulting shape may lack an obvious functional form; it separately reports collapse onto a schedule-specific curve.
rows.check: The state should be 'observed' for V7: the schedule-dependence and departure from a power-law form do appear. The result concerns per-run loss-versus-tokens curves under decay schedules. The text reports it qualitatively, with no fit statistic.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-5M pixel-token transformers, chess transformers and MLP synthetic regression, at small scale
relationships.reason: Compute-frontier fits of the form L0+ac^-b and joint t^-μ+p^-ν fits with R²≈0.998–0.999 hold in each setting (r1–r4).
relationships.display_finding: Offset compute-frontier power laws and joint training-step and parameter power laws fitted each setting with R² approximately 0.998–0.999.

relationships.condition: Transformer ladders spanning about one decade of compute; chess; decay schedules
relationships.reason: The transformer fits cover a narrow range (r1, r3), and the chess fit is worse than the others (r3). The sum-of-power-laws form fails for per-run curves under most learning-rate schedules (r11).
relationships.display_finding: Transformer fits spanned about one compute decade, chess fit less well than other settings, and sums of power laws failed to describe individual runs under most learning-rate schedules.

relationships.condition: Compute-optimal frontiers from constant-learning-rate runs in three small-scale non-language tasks
relationships.reason: c*∝p^(1+γ) with γ≈0.96–1.04 in every task gives a stable, roughly equal parameter/token split, like Hoffmann et al. (r5–r7). Endpoint models are dropped and no uncertainty is given.
relationships.display_finding: The relationship c*∝p^(1+γ), with γ≈0.96–1.04 across tasks, implied roughly equal allocation growth after excluding endpoint models, without reported uncertainty.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-5M loss curves under learning-rate decay schedules
relationships.reason: The authors state the power-law form fails under most schedules and the curve shape may lack an obvious functional form (r11).
relationships.display_finding: The power-law form failed under most learning-rate schedules, and the resulting curves sometimes lacked an obvious functional form.
